newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ markets hold breath for MPS after budget.
newsitem.headline: NZ markets hold breath for MPS after budget.

text.p: New Zealand bonds came under slight selling pressure in the wake of the 1997/98 budget but the currency was unmoved and shares ended in positive territory.
Treasurer Winston Peters' moment in the limelight was brief, with markets now already focusing on Friday's Monetary Policy Statement from the Reserve Bank.

Dealers said the budget contained no large surprises, as lower operating surpluses and a higher government borrowing programme were well flagged, but the market had still been disappointed at the size of projected surpluses.
An hour after Peters had delivered his first budget the kiwi dollar was at US$0.6860/67 and the Trade-Weighted Index was at 67.28, both unchanged against levels prevailing before the budget.

The bonds, which had attracted some buying going into the budget, rose slightly in yield. By 3.45 p.m. (0345 GMT) the 11/06s were three basis points weaker at 7.04 percent, while the 02/01s were also off three at 6.85 percent.

"The bonds are coming under a little bit of pressure. I think the growth assumptions in the budget are probably a little on the optimistic side of where the market saw it," said Jim Reardon, senior manager of domestic markets at ANZ Bank.

"The surpluses are smaller than the market saw it, and overall I think we're seeing some degree of fiscal slippage in the sense that there is a lot more spending and a lot less emphasis on repayment of debt.
"I think the market had been looking for something a little bit better than that," Reardon said.
The government's projected surplus for 1997/98 fell to NZ$1.5 billion, from $3.3 billion projected in the March Budget Policy Statement (BPS).
Likewise, in the 1998/99 and 1999/00 years the surplus was seen at only $1.9 billion and $2.6 billion, against previous forecasts of $2.6 billion and $3.5 billion respectively.
The country's economic growth rate was seen peaking at 4.2 percent in the year to March 1999. In 1997/98 GDP growth was projected at 2.4 percent, against the March BPS forecast of 3.6 percent.

The Debt Management Office (DMO) announced a 1997/98 bond tender programme worth NZ$1.8 billion in total, including $300 million inflation-indexed bonds. Forecasts for the size of the programme had ranged from $1.2 billion to around $2 billion.
Bond dealers welcomed news that the DMO would launch a new 10-year benchmark bond, maturing on July 15, 2009.
"I imagine that over time it will become a reasonably attractive bond, once there's liquidity in it," Reardon said.

ANZ's Head of Foreign Exchange Bill Murdoch said there was nothing in the budget that was likely to alter Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash's view of the economy when he delivers the six-monthly Monetary Policy Statement on Friday.
Sharebrokers said there was nothing equity-specific in the budget that was likely to influence stocks.
The top 40 share index ended 7.63 points higher at 2,410.15 on aggressive buying in Telecom and Brierley Investments.
